title: Starry Night Over the Rhône
labelText: Painted on the bank of the Rhône at Arles in September 1888, at a spot a minute or two from the house Van Gogh was renting on the place Lamartine. The gas lamps of the town burn across the water in ragged columns of gold; overhead the Great Bear sparkles green and pink against an aquamarine sky. Van Gogh worked at night, on the spot, under a gas jet — fascinated, he wrote to his brother Theo, by the problem of painting the night not as black, but as colour richer than the day's.
extendedNote:
The night sky had been on Van Gogh's mind for months before this canvas. From Arles in the spring of 1888 he wrote to Émile Bernard that a starry night was the picture he wanted to paint, 'in the same way as in the day I'll try to paint a green meadow studded with dandelions.' The difficulty was practical as much as poetic: how to see one's palette in the dark. His solution, that September, was to work under gaslight at the river's edge, where the new municipal lamps of Arles threw their own light into the scene he was painting.

What resulted is a picture of two kinds of light. The stars — he took care that the Great Bear should be recognisable — flare in soft bursts of white, green and rose, laid on in short separated strokes. Below them the gaslight of the town runs molten across the river, gold dragged down through royal blue in long vertical reflections. Between the two zones the Rhône itself turns like shot silk. In the foreground, almost an afterthought, a pair of lovers walks at the water's edge — the note of ordinary human warmth Van Gogh rarely omitted from even his most visionary pictures.

He described the painting precisely in a letter to Theo: the sky aquamarine, the water royal blue, the ground mauve; the town blue and violet; the gas yellow, its reflections russet-gold shading down to bronze-green. The precision matters. This is not a hallucination but an observation, made by a painter who believed the night was 'more alive and more richly coloured than the day.' Nine months later, in the asylum at Saint-Rémy, he would paint the other, more famous starry night from memory and imagination. This one was painted from the world, with wet feet, by lamplight. It entered the national collection in 1975 and hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.
